content: Insulin glargine is a synthetic, long-acting form of human insulin used to manage blood sugar levels in individuals with type 1 diabetes (a condition where the body does not produce insulin) and type 2 diabetes (a condition where the body does not use insulin effectively). It is prescribed for patients who require long-acting insulin to control their diabetes. Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas that facilitates the movement of sugar from the bloodstream into body tissues for energy use and helps metabolize carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. In diabetes, the pancreas does not produce sufficient insulin, necessitating the use of additional insulin to meet the body’s needs. Uncontrolled diabetes can lead to severe complications, including nerve damage, blood vessel issues, kidney problems, and vision loss. Insulin glargine is administered as a subcutaneous injection (under the skin, not into a vein) once daily, typically at bedtime. It is available in vials and prefilled cartridges. The dosage depends on factors such as diet, exercise, other medications, and concurrent illnesses, and it may change over time. Your doctor will determine the appropriate dose for you. Follow the prescription instructions carefully and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Do not take more or less insulin than prescribed, and do not stop using it without consulting your doctor. Insulin glargine helps control diabetes but does not cure it, so it must be taken regularly, even if you feel well. Do not shake the vial or cartridge before use, and do not dilute or mix insulin glargine with other insulins or solutions. Use a clean syringe without any residue from other medications. If using cartridges, only use the OptiPen One Insulin Delivery Device, and read the accompanying instructions before use. Have your healthcare provider demonstrate the correct technique and practice under their supervision. If using vials, you will need to withdraw the medication into a syringe. Use a syringe marked for U-100 insulin products to avoid dosing errors. Disposable plastic syringes should be used only once, as reused needles can cause pain or infection. Never share needles or syringes. To withdraw insulin glargine, wash your hands, warm the vial in your hands, and inspect the medication to ensure it is clear and colorless. If it appears cloudy or contains particles, discard the vial. If using a new vial, remove the protective cap but not the rubber stopper, and clean the top with alcohol. Inject air into the vial equal to the dose you need, then withdraw the insulin into the syringe, ensuring there are no air bubbles. If bubbles are present, tap the syringe to release them and adjust the dose. Once ready, inject the insulin subcutaneously. Choose an injection site, such as the abdomen, buttocks, thighs, or arms, and clean the area with alcohol. Pinch a fold of skin and insert the needle at a 45to 90-degree angle. Slowly push the plunger to inject all the insulin, leaving the needle in place for a few seconds before removing it. Press lightly on the injection site without rubbing. Dispose of needles and syringes according to instructions. Rotate injection sites within the same general area (e.g., the thigh) to avoid using the same site more than once a month. Before using insulin glargine, inform your doctor if you are allergic to insulin or other medications, and provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs, vitamins, and supplements you are taking. Certain medications, such as ACE inhibitors, corticosteroids, and oral diabetes drugs, may interact with insulin glargine. Notify your doctor if you have a history of thyroid, liver, or kidney disease, or if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while using insulin glargine, contact your doctor immediately. Inform your healthcare provider if you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, or if you experience fever, infection, injury, or illness with vomiting or diarrhea, as these conditions can affect blood sugar levels. Follow your doctor’s dietary and exercise recommendations, and do not start a new diet or exercise program without consulting them, as your insulin dose may need adjustment. Alcohol can lower blood sugar levels, so discuss safe alcohol consumption with your doctor. If you miss a dose or accidentally take an extra dose, consult your doctor for specific instructions. Write these instructions down for future reference. Insulin glargine may cause changes in blood sugar levels. Be aware of the symptoms of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), such as shakiness, dizziness, sweating, irritability, headache, numbness around the mouth, weakness, pale skin, hunger, or clumsy movements. Severe hypoglycemia can lead to confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness. If you experience symptoms of hypoglycemia, check your blood sugar and consume a sugary food or drink, such as fruit juice or candy. Inform your family and friends about these symptoms so they can seek medical help if needed. Symptoms of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) include extreme thirst, frequent urination, extreme hunger, weakness, and blurred vision. Untreated hyperglycemia can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening condition characterized by dry mouth, upset stomach, vomiting, fruity-smelling breath, and decreased consciousness. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience these symptoms. Common side effects of insulin glargine include redness, swelling, pain, or itching at the injection site, as well as changes in skin texture, such as thickening or depressions. Severe side effects, such as exaggerated sunburn, difficulty speaking or moving, widespread rash or hives, swelling of the hands or feet, difficulty swallowing, wheezing, rapid pulse, or low blood pressure, require immediate medical attention. Store unopened insulin glargine vials and cartridges in the refrigerator, but do not freeze them. Do not use insulin that has been frozen or exposed to extreme heat. Refrigerated insulin can be stored until the expiration date on the label. If refrigeration is unavailable, store insulin at room temperature away from direct sunlight and extreme heat. Unrefrigerated 10-mL vials or cartridges can be used within 28 days, while 5-mL vials can be used within 14 days. Once a cartridge is placed in the OptiPen device, do not refrigerate it. Discard any insulin exposed to extreme conditions or that is expired. Consult your pharmacist for proper disposal of unused medication. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual collapses or stops breathing. Keep all medical appointments and regularly monitor your blood sugar and HbA1c levels to assess your response to insulin glargine. Your doctor will guide you on how to check your blood or urine sugar levels at home. Adjustments to your insulin dose may be necessary during illness, stress, weight changes, or changes in diet or exercise. Notify your doctor of any such changes. Maintain good hygiene, clean wounds promptly, and wear medical alert identification indicating you have diabetes. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist for any questions about refilling your prescription.
